data.title: Prolonged rapamycin treatment inhibits mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB
data.authors: Sarbassov DD; Ali SM; Sengupta S; Sheen JH; Hsu PP; Bagley AF; Markhard AL; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: The molecular explanation for rapamycin's dark side. Short-term rapamycin only hits mTORC1, but LONG-term treatment also strips down mTORC2 in many cells, cutting Akt signaling. This is the mechanistic root of the insulin-resistance side effect later shown in mice (see Lamming 2012) - crucial for anyone dosing rapamycin for longevity.
data.abstract_excerpt: The drug rapamycin has important uses in oncology, cardiology, and transplantation medicine, but its clinically relevant molecular effects are not understood. When bound to FKBP12, rapamycin interacts with and inhibits the kinase activity of a multiprotein complex composed of mTOR, mLST8, and raptor (mTORC1). The distinct complex of mTOR, mLST8, and rictor (mTORC2) does not interact with FKBP12-rapamycin and is not thought to be rapamycin sensitive. mTORC2 phosphorylates and activates Akt/PKB, a key regulator of cell survival.

extracted_findings.effect: Prolonged rapamycin inhibits mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB in some cells – mTORC2 is not always rapamycin-insensitive
